fixes.explanation: Right, friend. David says, "Your tongue devises destruction like a sharpened razor…" (Psalm 52:2). Devises means he's planning it out, not just stumbling into it. A razor is the picture David gives for this tongue.

Yes, friend. David says, "You love every word that devours, O deceitful tongue." (Psalm 52:4). Devours is a hungry word, like something being swallowed up whole. That's the kind of word this tongue loves.

Heals would be a lovely word, friend, but it's the opposite of what David says. He says, "You love every word that devours, O deceitful tongue." (Psalm 52:4). Devours is the word, and it's not a mending kind of word.

Soothing words are the kind you'd want on a rough day, friend. But David says the opposite: "You love every word that devours, O deceitful tongue." (Psalm 52:4). Devours is the word. Nothing soothing about it.

Withering is a fair guess after that uprooting talk, friend, but it's not David's word. He says, "But I am like an olive tree flourishing in the house of God…" (Psalm 52:8). The uprooting is for the mighty man in verse 5. David calls himself flourishing.

Hidden is a fun guess, friend, but it's not in the verse. David says, "But I am like an olive tree flourishing in the house of God…" (Psalm 52:8). The word he uses is flourishing. That's a tree doing well.

Becoming king is a big deal, friend. I'd throw a parade and wear my tallest hat. But David doesn't give that as his reason. He says, "I will praise You forever, because You have done it." (Psalm 52:9). His reason is what God has done.

Yes, friend. David says, "I will wait on Your name—for it is good—in the presence of Your saints." (Psalm 52:9). He says he will wait in the presence of God's saints. I think waiting with company sounds a lot easier.

Waiting alone sounds lonely, friend, and that's not what David says. He says, "I will wait on Your name—for it is good—in the presence of Your saints." (Psalm 52:9). The place he names is the presence of God's saints.

Saul's court is a clever guess, friend, since Saul is in the story behind this psalm. But David doesn't say that here. He says, "I will wait on Your name—for it is good—in the presence of Your saints." (Psalm 52:9). The place he names is the presence of God's saints.
